report.source_text: On initial assessment at ED, he appeared confused. He demonstrated loss of ability to speak or read English, though he did not display visual agnosia when prompted in Thai (translated by his family). He exhibited severe slurring of speech, dysgraphia and ataxic gait. There was no facial asymmetry. Extraocular movements were intact. He was slow to obeying commands and demonstrated loss of ability to perform complex tasks such as drawing a full clock, though he was able to perform one-command tasks when prompted in Thai. Full cranial nerve examination revealed left-sided visual neglect. He had grossly normal tone, power, sensation and reflexes. Babinski reflexes were absent. He could only mobilise with one assist on seat-walker due to ataxic gait. No myoclonic jerks were identified.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) - confirmed on postmortem brain autopsy
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 76-year-old Thai migrant man, previously cognitively and physically well, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of sudden-onset motor, functional, and cognitive decline characterized by confusion, memory loss, visual deficit, and gait unsteadiness. Initial presentation included severe speech slurring, dysgraphia, ataxic gait, and left-sided visual neglect, with preserved language comprehension in Thai but loss of English language ability. Neurological examination showed no focal motor deficits, pyramidal signs, or myoclonic jerks initially, with grossly normal tone, power, sensation, and reflexes. Initial CT brain was normal, excluding acute stroke or hemorrhage. MRI brain on day 1 after admission revealed bilateral cortical ribboning on diffusion-weighted images (DWI) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), highly suggestive of sporadic CJD (sCJD). EEG on day 6 showed diffuse encephalopathy pattern with posterior dominant rhythm in the 5-7 Hz range, delta activity (1-2 Hz), and theta activity, without typical periodic sharp wave complexes. By day 7, the patient demonstrated markedly rapid cognitive decline with severe agitation, akinetic mutism, aphasia, echolalia, echopraxia, limb stiffness, and upper limb myoclonic jerks. Functional decline was severe, progressing to bedbound state with incontinence and loss of swallowing function requiring nasogastric feeding. RUDAS cognitive score was 0 by day 7. Repeat MRI on day 10 showed no significant interval change in the cortical ribboning pattern despite severe clinical deterioration. By day 14, nasogastric feeding was ceased, and the patient was referred to palliative care. The patient died on day 17 postadmission. Postmortem brain autopsy confirmed the diagnosis of CJD.
